opus-5.5.text:
Watching that lab come together was really eye-opening for me. When you're a student, you tend to see a research group as something that already exists: the people, the projects, the culture. But seeing Andreas build it almost from scratch, I realized how many deliberate choices go into it. What questions do you bet on? Who do you bring in? How do you get people from very different backgrounds, some from neuroscience, some from physics, some from machine learning, to actually talk to each other rather than just sit in the same building?

What struck me most was the conviction behind it. Neuroscience and AI have this long, tangled history. People keep saying the brain should inspire better models, or that models can help us understand the brain, but it's often more slogan than practice. Andreas seemed to take it seriously as a scientific program, not just a branding exercise. He was willing to spend years setting up infrastructure, data pipelines, and collaborations before the exciting results came out. That patience was something I didn't fully appreciate before.

It also changed how I think about my own work. I come more from the physics and interpretability side, and I've always cared about understanding *why* a model works, not just *that* it works. Seeing a lab organized around understanding an intelligent system, in this case the brain, made me feel that what I'm doing with neural networks is part of the same broader quest. Whether the system is biological or artificial, you face similar problems: it's high-dimensional, it's messy, and you need both good tools and good taste in questions.

And on a personal level, it made me think about what kind of researcher I want to be in the long run. Not just someone who writes papers, but maybe someday someone who can build an environment where other people can do their best work. That's a very different skill, and watching it up close was a kind of education you don't get from reading papers.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it affected me more than I expected. When I first saw Andreas putting the lab together, my instinct as a physicist was a bit skeptical. Neuroscience always felt messy to me, lots of data, very few clean equations. But watching how he framed the questions changed my mind. He wasn't asking "how do we make a model that fits neural recordings." He was asking "what is the brain actually computing, and can we write that down in a way a person can understand." That is exactly the question I care about on the AI side.

What really struck me was the way the lab treated interpretability as a shared problem rather than two separate fields. Neuroscientists have spent decades trying to read out meaning from neurons they didn't design. We in machine learning now have networks we did design, and we still can't read them. Seeing that parallel up close made me feel that the tools should flow both ways. Some of the thinking behind KANs, the idea that you want learnable functions you can actually look at and name, got sharper for me after those conversations.

It also shifted how I think about what counts as a result. In physics, a result is a law. In Andreas's group, a result could be a mechanism, a circuit, a story about why a population of cells behaves the way it does. That gave me permission to value explanations that aren't a single beautiful formula, as long as they are genuinely understandable. So I would say it made me more humble about the brain and more ambitious about AI at the same time.
